prompt: In `resource "aws_vpc" "shop" { ... }`, what is `shop`?
hint: A resource block takes two labels.

choices.text: The resource type, which picks the provider's schema
choices.why: That is `aws_vpc`, the first label.

choices.text: The name label
choices.why: Yes. It is the name Ana chose, and with the type it makes the address `aws_vpc.shop`.

choices.text: An argument whose value is a string
choices.why: An argument has an equals sign; a label sits in the block's header.

choices.text: The tag AWS shows as the VPC's Name
choices.why: The label never reaches AWS; the Name tag comes from `tags`.

prompt: Why can `tags = merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "shop" })` be written, while a nested block like `lifecycle { ... }` cannot be produced by a function?
hint: Look for the equals sign.

choices.text: `tags` is an argument whose value is a map, and a value comes from any expression
choices.why: Right. A block is structure in the file; an argument holds a value, and values can be computed.

choices.text: `merge` is a special form reserved for tags
choices.why: `merge` works on any maps; the lesson used it on two literal ones in the console.

choices.text: Blocks are read before functions are loaded
choices.why: There is no such loading order; the difference is between a value and a structure.

choices.text: Because `lifecycle` belongs to Terraform and `tags` to AWS
choices.why: Who reads it is not the point; `required_providers` is Terraform's too and is a block for the same reason.

prompt: Ana splits her configuration into `main.tf`, `network.tf` and `owner.tf.json` in one directory. What does Terraform do with them?
hint: The file names are a convention.

choices.text: Reads `main.tf` first, then the rest in the order they are referenced
choices.why: `main.tf` has no special status; its name is a convention for people.

choices.text: Refuses the JSON file unless every file is JSON
choices.why: The lesson's `validate` passed with both kinds in one directory.

choices.text: Treats each file as a separate module
choices.why: A module is a directory, not a file; that is lesson 10.

choices.text: Reads all three as one configuration
choices.why: Yes: every `.tf` and `.tf.json` in the directory, in no meaningful order.

prompt: Before anything was applied, `aws_vpc.shop.cidr_block` in the console printed `(known after apply)`, though the file says `"10.20.0.0/16"`. Why?
hint: Where does the console read a resource from?

choices.text: The console reads resources from the state, and there was none
choices.why: Right. A resource's values come from the state; with nothing applied, Terraform writes the placeholder.

choices.text: moto was not running
choices.why: The console asks AWS nothing; it evaluates against the configuration and the state.

choices.text: The CIDR was invalid
choices.why: The same range was applied a section later without complaint.

choices.text: A quoted string is evaluated only during apply
choices.why: `"shop-${var.environment}"` was evaluated in the same console a line earlier.

prompt: HCL has no `if` statement. To choose between two values it uses the conditional operator, written `condition ___ a : b`.
hint: One character.

prompt: A colleague writes an IAM policy as JSON inside a `<<-EOT` heredoc. What does the lesson suggest instead, and why?
hint: A heredoc is a string.

choices.text: `<<EOT`, so the indentation is kept
choices.why: Indentation is not the problem; either form is still an unchecked string.

choices.text: `jsonencode()` of a real value, which cannot produce broken JSON
choices.why: Yes. A missing comma in a heredoc is found by AWS; a value passed to `jsonencode` cannot have one.

choices.text: A `%{for}` directive per statement
choices.why: That builds the same string by hand, with more ways to get it wrong.

choices.text: A `.tf.json` file for the policy
choices.why: `.tf.json` is another way to write the configuration, not a policy document.

prompt: What does `cidrsubnet("10.20.0.0/16", 8, 2)` return?
hint: Eight new bits, network number 2.

choices.why: That would be two new bits; the second argument is how many bits are added.
The 8 is the number of new bits, not the subnet's number.
Right: a /16 plus 8 bits is a /24, and number 2 has 2 in the third octet.
That is a host address, which `cidrhost` returns.

prompt: With `cidrsubnet("10.20.0.0/16", 8, netnum)`, how many different subnets can `netnum` choose from?
hint: Two to the power of the new bits.

prompt: `merge({ Project = "shop", Owner = "ana" }, { Owner = "bruno" })` returns what for `Owner`?
hint: Which map wins on a shared key?

choices.text: An error about a duplicate key
choices.why: That error belongs to a `for` expression building a map; `merge` resolves duplicates.

choices.text: A list holding both owners
choices.why: Grouping into lists is what `...` does in a `for`; `merge` keeps one value.

choices.text: `"ana"`, because the first map sets the defaults
choices.why: It is the other way round, which is what makes the second map an override.

choices.text: `"bruno"`
choices.why: Yes: the later map wins, and `Project` is kept from the first.

prompt: A validation rule must accept any string that is a valid CIDR range and refuse everything else. `cidrnetmask(var.cidr)` errors on an invalid one. What should the condition be?
hint: A condition must be true or false.

choices.text: `try(cidrnetmask(var.cidr), false)`
choices.why: For a valid range this returns a mask string, not `true`, so the condition is not a boolean.

choices.text: `can(cidrnetmask(var.cidr))`
choices.why: Right: `can` turns "would this fail" into `false` or `true`, the shape the lesson's own rule uses.

choices.text: `!can(cidrnetmask(var.cidr))`
choices.why: That is the rule upside down: it refuses every valid range and accepts every invalid one.

choices.text: `cidrnetmask(var.cidr) != null`
choices.why: An invalid range makes the call fail, so the comparison is never reached and the error escapes.

prompt: Ana runs `terraform plan -var name=shop-test`, where `name` is a local. What happens?
hint: Who can reach a local?

choices.text: The local takes the new value for this run
choices.why: Only variables are inputs; a local is internal.

choices.text: An error: no variable of that name is declared
choices.why: Yes, "Value for undeclared variable": `-var` only reaches variable blocks.

choices.text: A warning, and the plan uses the local's value
choices.why: It was an error, and no plan was made.

choices.text: Terraform creates a variable called `name`
choices.why: Terraform never declares anything for you; it said to add a variable block.

prompt: Which of these should be a local rather than a variable, by the lesson's rule? Choose all that apply.
hint: Is it a choice for whoever runs Terraform, or derived?

choices.text: The environment, `dev` or `prod`
choices.why: That is a choice the person running Terraform makes: a variable.

choices.text: The name `shop-dev`, built from the environment
choices.why: Derived from other values: a local.

choices.text: The `Project = "shop"` tag on every resource
choices.why: A fact that should not be overridden: a local.

choices.text: The network's CIDR range
choices.why: The lesson names it as a choice for whoever runs Terraform.

choices.text: The map of common tags merged into each resource
choices.why: Used everywhere and derived: exactly `local.common_tags`.

prompt: Somebody adds `locals { vpc_cidr = "10.20.0.0/16" }` and uses it once. What does the lesson say about it?
hint: When does a local earn its place?

choices.text: It is required, since literals in resources are forbidden
choices.why: The VPC in `main.tf` still has a literal range, and it is valid.

choices.text: It only adds a jump for the reader
choices.why: Yes: used once, and its name says nothing the value does not.

choices.text: It makes the value settable from the command line
choices.why: No local can be set from outside; the lesson showed the error.

choices.text: It turns the VPC's range into a computed value that appears as `(known after apply)` in the plan
choices.why: A local made of a literal is known at plan time; the subnets' ranges were printed in full.

prompt: The `network` default left out `public`, declared as `optional(bool, false)`. What did `var.network.public` hold?
hint: The console printed the whole object.

choices.text: `null`
choices.why: That is what `optional(bool)` without a second argument gives.

choices.text: `false`
choices.why: Yes, filled in from the declaration's default.

choices.text: An error on read, since the attribute is missing
choices.why: An optional attribute is always present after conversion; that is its purpose.

choices.text: `true`
choices.why: The default in the declaration is `false`.

prompt: Match each type to what it holds.
hint: Collections have one element type; structural types have a shape.

pairs.right: Strings in order, any number of them
Strings with no order and no duplicates
Named attributes, each with its own type

prompt: In the console, `"5" + 1` gave `6` and `tonumber("three")` failed. What rule explains both?
hint: When can a conversion lose nothing?

choices.text: Arithmetic ignores types
choices.why: It does not: `"three" + 1` would fail for the same reason `tonumber` did.

choices.text: Strings convert to numbers only inside functions
choices.why: `"5" + 1` converted with no function at all.

choices.text: Terraform converts a value when the conversion is exact, and refuses when it is not
choices.why: Right: `"5"` is a number written as a string; `"three"` is not a decimal number.

choices.text: `tonumber` is stricter than `+`, which rounds
choices.why: Nothing was rounded; both use the same conversion.

prompt: What does `{ for i, az in var.network.azs : az => cidrsubnet(var.network.cidr, 8, i + 1) }` produce?
hint: Braces, and an arrow.

choices.text: A list of two ranges
choices.why: Square brackets make a list; these are braces.

choices.text: A map from zone to range
Two subnets in AWS, one per zone
choices.why: An expression produces a value and creates nothing; creating one per entry is `for_each`, lesson 4.

choices.text: A map from index to zone
choices.why: The key is `az` and the value the range; `i` only feeds `cidrsubnet`.

prompt: `{ for az in var.network.azs : substr(az, 0, 9) => az }` failed with "Duplicate object key". What did adding `...` after the value change?
hint: Two zones, one region.

choices.text: The second zone overwrote the first
choices.why: A `for` never overwrites silently; it errors, or with `...` it groups.

choices.text: Duplicates were dropped, as `toset` does
choices.why: Both zones were kept in the result.

choices.text: The key became the full zone name
choices.why: The key expression did not change; `substr` still cut it to `sa-east-1`.

choices.text: Each key now holds a list of every zone that produced it
choices.why: Right: `"sa-east-1" = ["sa-east-1a", "sa-east-1c"]`.

prompt: `[aws_subnet.a, aws_subnet.c][___].cidr_block` reads `cidr_block` from both subnets; it is short for a `for` expression.
hint: The splat operator.

prompt: `terraform plan -var environment=staging` failed on the validation rule. What had Terraform planned or changed by then?
hint: The figure puts validation before the plan.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Yes: the value was refused as it arrived, with Ana's message.

choices.text: The VPC's tags, which do not depend on the environment
choices.why: They do depend on it, through `local.common_tags`, and nothing was planned anyway.

choices.text: A plan, shown with a warning at the end
choices.why: A warning with a plan is what a check block gives; validation is an error.

choices.text: Every resource except the ones that read `var.environment`
choices.why: A failed variable stops the whole run, not a part of it.

prompt: Why is the bucket name's length checked in a precondition rather than in a variable's validation?
hint: Where does the name come from?

choices.text: Validation rules cannot call `length`
choices.why: Any function works in a condition; `can` and `cidrsubnet` did.

choices.text: Preconditions run after S3 answers
choices.why: It failed during the plan, before anything reached S3.

choices.text: The name is built from three pieces that no single variable holds
choices.why: Right: it lives in `local.bucket`, and the rule belongs beside the resource that uses it.

choices.text: A precondition only warns, and length is not worth an error
choices.why: It was an error, "Resource precondition failed"; only a check block warns.

prompt: Put these in the order Terraform meets them in a run where every one of them is used.
hint: Values arrive, then the plan, then the apply.
items: A postcondition on a value only known after the change
trap: A postcondition on an unknown value cannot run before the change: there is nothing to check yet.

prompt: What happened when the plan ran with the same zone given twice and the `two_zones` check failed? Choose all that apply.
hint: A check block is not an error.

choices.text: The plan stopped with an error
choices.why: It printed a full plan and a warning.

choices.text: A warning printed Ana's message
choices.why: Yes, "Check block assertion failed" with her sentence.

choices.text: The plan proposed replacing subnet `c`
choices.why: Yes: a new zone forces a new subnet, `-/+`.

choices.text: Terraform removed the duplicate zone itself
choices.why: It changed nothing about the input; `distinct` was only inside the condition.

prompt: A teammate replaces `cidr_block = cidrsubnet(var.network.cidr, 8, 1)` with the literal `"10.20.1.0/24"`, saying it is easier to read. Later the VPC moves to `10.30.0.0/16`. What is the consequence?
hint: Two places now state one fact.

choices.text: The subnet follows the VPC, as before
choices.why: A literal follows nothing; that was the point of computing it.

choices.text: Terraform rewrites the literal to match
choices.why: Terraform never edits your files.

choices.text: The subnet keeps a range outside the new VPC
choices.why: Right. The file now disagrees with itself, and AWS refuses the subnet when it is created.

choices.text: The validation rule on `network` catches the mismatch
choices.why: That rule checks only that the range has room for /24s; it never sees the subnet.

prompt: Ana wants `instance_type` to be `t3.large` in prod and `t3.micro` anywhere else, and an unknown environment should not be able to fail the lookup. Which expression fits?
hint: Two outcomes, one test.

choices.text: `lookup({ prod = "t3.large" }, var.environment)`
choices.why: Without a default, `dev` is a missing key and an error, as `staging` was in the lesson.

choices.text: `var.environment == "prod" ? "t3.large" : "t3.micro"`
choices.why: Yes. Two outcomes from one comparison is what the conditional operator is for, and it cannot fail on a key.

choices.text: `"t3.%{ if var.environment == "prod" }large%{ endif }"`
choices.why: Outside prod this gives `t3.`, which is not an instance type.

choices.text: `try(var.environment, "t3.micro")`
choices.why: Reading the variable never fails, so this returns the environment's name.

prompt: Match each error the lesson captured to what produced it.
hint: Read the first line of each, then the quoted line.

pairs.right: A string where a list was declared

prompt: Ana's output keyed subnets by `Name` tag, not by zone. With the same zone given twice, what would a zone-keyed output have done to the plan?
hint: Two items, one key, in a `for` building a map.

choices.text: Kept only the last subnet's range
choices.why: A `for` never overwrites silently.

choices.text: Added a second warning beside the check's
choices.why: A duplicate key is an error, not a warning.

choices.text: Nothing, since outputs are evaluated after apply
choices.why: Outputs are planned too; the lesson's apply showed "Changes to Outputs".

choices.text: Failed it with "Duplicate object key"
choices.why: Right: both subnets would claim `sa-east-1a`. That is why the key is the Name tag.
